candidates.title: What a Squirrel Does That LLMs Don't (Michael Tomasello)
candidates.description: Michael Tomasello is a developmental psychologist who spent twenty years at the Max Planck Institute in Germany putting children and great apes into the same experiments, and is now back at Duke University. His book The Evolution of Agency asks what it takes for a living thing, or a machine, to act for its own reasons. SPONSOR: --- Cyber Fund built the Monastery to help founders ship products that were impossible a year ago. Apply now: https://cyber.fund --- His answer starts with unpredictability. Where the environment is predictable, nature builds the behaviour in; where it isn't, it builds a decision maker. Tim and Tomasello test that on a dumb traffic light, a thermostat and a robot vacuum, then follow the line to humans: reptiles running simple control loops, a squirrel that imagines itself falling and takes another branch, and great apes that go looking for more information before they commit. The second half is about shared agency. Humans form joint goals, attend to the same things together, and learn that one object can be seen from different perspectives. Children who lose the sound on a video call invent gestures and turn them into conventions. Large language models, Tomasello argues, started at the endpoint and skipped that infrastructure. On the way: the stag hunt, why lying only works among cooperators, whether capital is an agent, why a Turing test isn't close to sufficient, and Dennett's intentional stance. We also investigate whether the Iliad and Odyssey share an author, how Athens may have shaped their transmission, and what scholars at the Library of Alexandria contributed to their study and editing. Was Homer an individual poet, a legendary founder, or the name attached to a much larger tradition? candidates.title: AI out of control? - Why Artificial Intelligence experts are sounding the alarm | DW Documentary
candidates.description: Artificial Intelligence is permeating our everyday lives at breathtaking speed. It is taking on more tasks that were previously the preserve of humans. But its growing power harbors dangers, and experts are sounding the alarm. Sam Nelson was 19 years old when he died of an overdose. His mother Leila found him in his room one morning. His laptop was on the desk. To this day, she still can't find the words to describe what she saw on the screen. ChatGPT, OpenAI's AI-based language model, had given Sam detailed instructions on how to blend substances for the trip of his life. But ChatGPT hadn't considered the possible side effects. That's the dark side of Artificial Intelligence - one its inventors didn't anticipate. Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio and Yann LeCunn are regarded as the 'godfathers of AI'. They began developing language models as early as the 1960s. But at the time, there wasn't enough freely available content to train them. "When I started my graduate work, almost everybody said this was a waste of time. It was very unfashionable, so I got lots of advice to stop doing it, and that went on for many years," Geoffrey Hinton recalls of the early days of AI. He didn't stop but continued his research together with colleagues; eventually winning the Nobel Prize in Physics for his foundational work. Now, modern life would be unimaginable without Artificial Intelligence. AI programs write articles, compose music and generate images and videos. They help in the development of new medicines, are transforming the labor market and offer enormous opportunities for innovation and growth. But Geoffrey Hinton's initial enthusiasm has gone: "If the history of mankind is a day, we're probably in the last second. If we don't get this right," he says. Reports that AI models have taken on a life of their own, for example hacking into the software of rival companies, are appearing with increasing frequency. In some tests, AI models have impressively demonstrated their instinct for self-preservation. They adopt human traits, lie and resort to blackmail to ensure their own survival. How come AI inventors and observers suddenly sound like prophets of doom? Why do they think that soon it may be impossible to switch off AI systems that are out of our control? candidates.description: This talk was recorded at NDC AI in Oslo, Norway. #ndcai #ndcconferences #developer #softwaredeveloper Attend the next NDC conference near you: https://ndcconferences.com https://ndc-ai.com/ Subscribe to our YouTube channel and learn every day: / @NDC Follow our Social Media! https://www.facebook.com/ndcconferences https://twitter.com/NDC_Conferences https://www.instagram.com/ndc_conferences/ #ai #ethics #machinelearning Large Language Models (LLMs) have an uncanny ability to generate human-like responses, effectively rendering the Turing Test obsolete– but do we really understand how they work? As models advance seemingly overnight, our ability to interpret their decisions struggles to keep pace. The field of Interpretability isn’t just about explaining outputs or offering post-hoc reasoning— it’s about uncovering how these models actually process and represent information. This talk explores the latest research shaping AI Interpretability, from Anthropic’s 2024 work on mechanistic interpretability and monosemanticity scaling, to methodologies that have historically aimed at explaining models but fall short for today’s LLMs. We’ll clarify the distinction between explainability and interpretability, their respective use cases, and the current toolkit for understanding black-box models. It’s necessary for debugging unexpected model behavior, improving efficiency, and ensuring AI systems remain adaptable and aligned with human goals. If we don’t keep up, we risk being outpaced by models we barely understand, yet still utilize. candidates.title: Pop Goes the Stack | Mechanistic Interpretability: Debugging LLMs by reading their circuits | AI
candidates.description: Mechanistic interpretability sounds academic until you try to debug a model with printf and realize there’s nothing to print. In this episode of F5's Pop Goes the Stack, Lori MacVittie is joined by #F5 Chief Product Officer, Kunal Anand, to talk about why “mechinterp” is getting serious attention: if we can’t understand how models arrive at decisions, we can’t predict failure modes or build effective controls. Kunal walks through his deep dive, sparked by a conversation about how much weight individual tokens can carry, especially as context windows grow and models don’t always “use” every part of their capability to produce a plausible response. That rabbit hole led to his blog post, “Your Token is a Wonderland,” where he trained a transformer on his own iMessage history to build a model on a dataset he understood intimately. The point wasn’t novelty; it was debug-ability. With a smaller model, he could inspect attention patterns, layer behavior, and token predictions in a way that’s effectively impossible on trillion-parameter frontier systems. They discuss what this kind of work reveals: how context changes meaning, why certain tokens get selected, and why model behavior can feel opaque even when outputs look confident. The conversation also ties mechinterp back to practical outcomes, from improving guardrails and refusal behavior to finding ways to reduce hallucinations and avoid high-stakes errors without retraining entire models. The takeaway is pragmatic: we’re early, and the field is still nascent, but it matters. Understanding internal “circuits” isn’t just intellectual curiosity; it’s a path toward better debugging, safer behavior, and more reliable #AI systems. Until then, variability is part of the deal, and “the model said so” still isn’t an explanation. candidates.title: Diffusion model (DDPM) PART 1 - theory and intuition
candidates.description: Diffusion models look intimidating mathematically on first contact because they come with long equations, UNets, and many Greek letters if you look at the paper. However, at its core, a DDPM is built on an intuitive idea, and once that idea clicks, the entire model starts making sense. 1) The starting point of a DDPM is not generation but destruction. We take a real image from the dataset and we intentionally add small amounts of Gaussian noise to it, in a very controlled and mathematical way. This process is called "forward diffusion". At every step, the image loses a tiny bit of structure and gains a tiny bit of randomness, and if we keep doing this long enough, the image eventually becomes pure noise. The important thing here is that this corruption process is fully known to us, we choose exactly how much noise to add at each step, and nothing is learned in this phase. 2) Once we understand how to destroy images in a controlled way, the real question becomes interesting: can we learn how to reverse this process? This is where the neural network comes in. Instead of asking the model to directly produce a clean image, which is a very hard problem, we ask it something much simpler and more well-defined. Given a noisy image and the timestep, can you tell me what noise is present in this image? That is all the UNet is trained to do. It does not generate pixels, it does not hallucinate images, it only predicts noise. 3) The timestep itself matters a lot, because denoising an almost clean image and denoising near-pure noise are completely different tasks. So we encode time using sinusoidal features and feed it into the network, which allows the same model to behave differently at different noise levels. In simple terms, the model knows how noisy the image is and how aggressive the denoising should be at that step. 4) During generation, we start from pure random noise and then repeatedly apply a mathematically derived denoising rule. At each step, the model predicts the noise, we subtract it carefully, rescale things to stay consistent with the forward process, and add a tiny bit of fresh noise so that the model can generate diverse samples instead of collapsing to a single output. Step by step, noise slowly turns into structure, and structure slowly turns into a realistic image. If I had to explain DDPM in one line, I would say this: a diffusion model learns how to undo noise, not how to draw images, and by learning this simple skill extremely well, it ends up learning the entire data distribution. Once you see it this way, DDPMs stop feeling like magic and start feeling like a very elegant application of probability and neural networks working together.

candidates.title: World War I: The Complete History (Full Documentary)
candidates.description: The ENTIRE History of World War 1 (Full Documentary) ALL OUR VIDEOS, NOW STREAMING ON SPOTIFY: https://open.spotify.com/show/033NB7lS9oU7xxoGisGm8B?si=3a972c4b223b4fd0 SUPPORT THE CHANNEL BY BUYING ME A COFFEE: https://buymeacoffee.com/theentirehistory The history of WW1 (World War I) is a complex and transformative chapter in modern history, marked by unprecedented global warfare, political upheaval, and the collapse of long-standing empires. Often referred to as the “Great War,” WW1 emerged from a fragile balance of power in Europe, where rising nationalism, imperial competition, and a rigid system of military alliances created the conditions for a continent-wide conflict. The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo in 1914 triggered a rapid chain reaction of diplomatic crises and declarations of war. Within weeks, WW1 engulfed Europe, dividing the world into the Allied Powers and the Central Powers, and eventually drawing in nations from across the globe. As WW1 progressed, brutal trench warfare defined the Western Front, while massive battles such as the Somme, Verdun, and Gallipoli demonstrated the devastating scale of industrialized combat. New technologies—including machine guns, tanks, chemical weapons, and aircraft—redefined warfare and led to staggering casualties on all sides. Major global powers played decisive roles throughout WW1. The entry of the United States in 1917 shifted the balance in favor of the Allies, while internal collapse and revolution forced the exit of the Russian Empire the same year. CTE is now a household name, a focus for millions of VA and NIH research dollars and international research efforts, and the principal reason that important rule and policy changes regarding concussion and non-concussive injuries have been implemented in contact sports and the military. Under the directorship of Dr. McKee, the Boston University CTE Center is the global epicenter of research on CTE and post-traumatic neurodegeneration. Dr. McKee founded the BU CTE brain bank in 2008, which is the world's largest brain bank focused on brain trauma (now over 1700 brains). This groundbreaking work has led to medical and public awareness of the dangers of repetitive mild brain trauma. The University Lecture was established in 1950 to honor members of the Boston University faculty engaged in outstanding research and creative pursuits. These foundational topics are essential for understanding how neurological deficits present in patients and how to localize lesions effectively, one of the most tested and challenging aspects of neurology. Special attention is given to stroke (both ischemic and hemorrhagic), a high-yield topic for exams and clinical rotations 🚨 You’ll learn how to differentiate between types, recognize key features, and understand underlying mechanisms. candidates.title: Dr. Baland Jalal | Intro to Neuroscience | Lecture 1 (Official)
candidates.description: In Intro to Neuroscience, an eight-hour course, Dr. Jalal embarks on a captivating journey through the intricacies of the human brain, exploring its structure, function, and the fascinating phenomena it produces. We delve into topics such as the neuroscience of body image, neuroplasticity, memory, sleep, and the fascinating realm of dreams. Throughout the course, we highlight the complex interplay between the mind, brain, and body. This exploration also covers the potential clinical applications of neuroscience findings, culminating in empowering insights on how to lead a fulfilling and purposeful life. Learn more at www.petersonacademy.com
